W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit dedicated to dismantling systemic barriers that prevent underserved communities from accessing technology, education, and economic opportunity. We serve first-generation learners, immigrants, refugees, and low-income youth and adults — communities historically underrepresented in technology and the workforce. Founded and led by educators with more than 30 years in the public school system, we've reached over 25,000 students across our chapters to date. Through coding education, digital literacy, career pathway development, and entrepreneurship support, we equip individuals with the critical skills needed to succeed in today's innovation economy — generating measurable, lasting economic impact. Digital Equity Workforce Readiness Innovation Economy Job Creation Economic Resilience Underserved Communities 🌍 Worldwide Reach Programs serving communities across the globe, with a focus on under-resourced regions. 💡 Tech & Innovation Bridging the digital divide with coding, creativity, and technology education. 📊 Economic Impact Measurable job creation, private investment, and long-term community prosperity. ✊ Equity First Every program designed to remove barriers and create genuine access to opportunity. Mission & Vision Why we exist, and who we serve. Our Mission To dismantle systemic barriers to technology, education, and economic opportunity by giving underserved learners the skills, credentials, and wrap-around support they need to build careers and lasting economic mobility. Our Vision A world where every learner, whatever their language, origin, or zip code, has a real path to meaningful work, financial stability, and leadership in their community. Who We Serve Refugees and immigrants, including newcomer families and English learners Underserved students, high school age and older Underserved women and girls Veterans First-generation and low-income youth and adults from vulnerable communities seeking economic mobility Wrap-around support for every learner Learning only works when the rest of life makes room for it. Alongside instruction, we support learners with: 🗣️ Language Access Interpretation, translation, and multilingual support for learners and their families. 🧑‍🏫 Mentoring & Coaching Regular check-ins, tutoring, and mentors who help learners finish what they start. 💻 Devices & Connectivity Help getting laptops and internet access, plus digital-literacy onboarding. 💼 Career Services Resume help, interview preparation, job readiness, and connections to employers. How we deliver W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is an independent, community-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization. We are not a school, a government agency, or a religious organization. Our programs are managed by dedicated program staff, supported by trained volunteers and chapter leads, and delivered through our chapters and partner organizations. That network gives us the capacity to enroll and support cohorts of 250 or more learners at a time. Where We Serve Rooted in Ohio. Growing across the country. W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is headquartered in West Chester, Ohio, and serves learners, families, and educators through community chapters in Kentucky, Florida, and Mississippi. Our impact reaches learners from 35 nations — and new communities join every year. Search wiseceo.org Search Esc News & Resources · October 16, 2026 · By Tiffany Davidson Your Child's IEP, Explained: A Family Guide to the Meeting Table What an IEP is, what your rights are, and the questions to bring — especially if your family speaks a language other than English at home Family Advocacy IEP & Special Education Education Access Every fall, families across Ohio sit down at a table with teachers, specialists and administrators to talk about one thing: how their child is going to learn this year. If you have ever walked out of an IEP meeting feeling rushed, confused or unheard, you are not alone — and you are not powerless. As an educator and literacy advocate, I have sat on every side of that table. This guide is the one I wish every family had before their first meeting. What is an IEP? An Individualized Education Program (IEP) is a written plan for a student who qualifies for special education under the federal law known as IDEA (the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act). It describes: How your child is doing right now (their "present levels") Measurable goals for the year The services, supports and accommodations the school will provide How progress will be measured and reported to you An IEP is not a label. It is a promise — in writing — about what your child will receive. Five rights every family should know You are a member of the IEP team. Not a guest. Your knowledge of your child counts as data. You can request an evaluation in writing. If you think your child needs help, put the request in an email or letter and keep a copy. You can ask for a meeting at any time. The IEP must be reviewed at least once a year, but you do not have to wait for the annual meeting if something is not working. You have the right to understand what is happening. If your family's primary language is not English, the school must take steps to make sure you understand the meeting — including arranging an interpreter. Ask for one ahead of time. You can take time before you sign. It is okay to say, "I'd like to take this home and review it." For families of English learners: A student can receive English language services and special education services at the same time. Learning English is not a disability — but a student who is learning English can also have a disability. If you are told your child has to "wait until their English improves" before being evaluated, ask the team to explain that decision in writing. Questions to bring to the table What do my child's assessment results actually show, in plain language? Which goal matters most this year, and how will we know it is working? How often will my child receive each service, and who provides it? What accommodations will my child have in class and on tests? How and how often will I get progress updates? What can we do at home to support the goals? Literacy belongs in the IEP conversation Reading touches every subject — science labs, word problems, history, even the instructions on a test. If your child is struggling with reading, ask the team directly: What does my child's reading data show, what is the specific skill gap, and what research-based intervention will close it? Vague answers like "we'll keep an eye on it" are a signal to ask for more detail. A simple routine before every meeting Ask for draft documents a few days early. Write down your top three concerns and your child's top three strengths. Bring a support person — a relative, friend or advocate. Take notes, and ask for a copy of everything you sign. Ohio resources Ohio families can find the state's parent guide to special education, Whose IDEA Is This? , through the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, and free training and support through the Ohio Coalition for the Education of Children with Disabilities (OCECD), Ohio's federally funded parent center. Search wiseceo.org Search Esc News & Resources · October 17, 2026 · By Tiffany Davidson Reading Is the First Job Skill: Why Literacy Is Workforce Development Every career pathway — healthcare, manufacturing, the trades, technology — starts with reading. Here's how families can build it at home, at any age. Literacy Workforce Development Family Advocacy When people talk about workforce development, they usually picture welding booths, hospital simulation labs or coding bootcamps. Those matter. But long before anyone earns a credential, there is a skill underneath every single one of them: reading. A nursing student reads medication orders. An apprentice electrician reads code requirements and wiring diagrams. A lab technician reads safety data sheets. A small-business owner reads contracts, loan terms and tax forms. Literacy is not separate from economic mobility — it is the foundation of it. What "literacy" really means today Literacy is more than sounding out words. It includes: Decoding and fluency — reading words accurately and smoothly Vocabulary — knowing what words mean, including the technical words of a field Comprehension — understanding, remembering and questioning what you read Writing — explaining your thinking clearly Digital literacy — finding, judging and using information online Five habits families can start this week Read together for 15 minutes a day. Any book, any language. Reading in your home language builds the same thinking skills — and those skills transfer to English. Talk about what you read. Ask, "What do you think will happen next?" or "Why did they do that?" Conversation builds comprehension. Collect "big words." When your child meets a new word, write it on a sticky note and use it at dinner. Vocabulary grows through use. Read the real world. Recipes, bus schedules, job postings, instructions for a new phone. Show kids that reading gets things done. Get a library card. Ohio's public libraries offer free books, e-books, homework help and computer access. For teens and young adults: Pick one career you are curious about and read three things from that field this month — a job posting, an article and a training program description. Circle every word you don't know. That list is your career vocabulary, and learning it puts you ahead. When to ask for help If your child avoids reading, guesses at words, reads slowly and tiredly, or understands much more when you read to them than when they read alone, those are signals worth sharing with their teacher. Ask what the school's reading assessments show and what support is available. Early help works — and it is never too late to start. Search wiseceo.org Search Esc News & Resources · October 18, 2026 · By Tiffany Davidson Six SIOP Moves Every Teacher Can Use Tomorrow With English Learners Practical, research-based strategies from a literacy advocate and ESL educator — no new curriculum required Literacy English Learners Teacher Strategies English learners are one of the fastest-growing groups of students in Ohio classrooms — and one of the most underserved. The good news: the strategies that help English learners succeed make lessons clearer for every student. The SIOP Model (Sheltered Instruction Observation Protocol) is a research-based framework for teaching content and academic language at the same time. It has eight components: Lesson Preparation, Building Background, Comprehensible Input, Strategies, Interaction, Practice & Application, Lesson Delivery, and Review & Assessment. You don't need to master all eight at once. Start with these six moves. 1. Post a language objective next to your content objective Content objective: "Students will explain how the water cycle works." Language objective: "Students will use sequence words — first, next, then, finally — to describe the water cycle orally and in writing." When students know what language they're practicing, they use it on purpose. 2. Pre-teach five words, not twenty-five Choose the few words students truly need to access the lesson. Show a picture, act it out, connect it to a home-language word when you can, and keep the words visible on a word wall all week. 3. Give sentence frames for academic talk "I agree with ___ because ___." "The evidence that shows ___ is ___." "One difference between ___ and ___ is ___." Frames lower the risk of speaking and raise the level of the conversation. 4. Make input comprehensible Slow down, pause, and use visuals, gestures, models and real objects. Write key directions on the board as well as saying them, and model the task before students try it. 5. Structure interaction every 10 minutes Turn-and-talk, Think-Pair-Share, numbered heads — short, structured talk gives every learner practice using new language, not just the confident few. 6. Check understanding without asking "Does everyone get it?" Use thumbs up/sideways/down, whiteboards, quick exit tickets or "show me with your fingers." Then reteach right away for students who need it. Coach's tip: Pick one move this week and use it in every lesson. Ask a colleague to watch for it. Small, consistent changes beat big one-time overhauls. Remember the families A student's home language is an asset, not an obstacle. Encourage families to read, talk and tell stories at home in the language they know best — strong first-language skills support English literacy. Teaching with you, Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed. Search wiseceo.org Search Esc News & Resources · October 15, 2026 · By Tiffany Davidson Taxing the Unbanked: Why Ohio Should Protect Check-Cashing and Payday Borrowers A proposed revenue idea, more than a decade of Ohio reform, and the protections every borrower can use today Policy Financial Capability Ohio By Tiffany Davidson, Founder and CEO, Worldwide Institute For Success And Excellence (W.I.S.E.C.E.O.) States and school districts are always looking for new revenue, and some ideas sound easy until you ask who would pay. One proposal that comes up in school finance discussions is a tax on people who cash checks or borrow at storefront lenders, charged on the size of the check or the amount borrowed. I recently evaluated that idea against the standard tests for a revenue source, and the answer was clear. It would raise little money, and it would collect that money from the households with the least. This article has two parts. The first explains why this tax works against Ohio's own policy. The second is a practical guide for anyone using these lenders today. Part 1: Why this tax falls on the wrong people A small base made up of struggling households In 2023, about 4.2 percent of U.S. households had no bank account, and another 14.2 percent had an account but still used services such as check cashing or payday loans (FDIC, 2024). These households are concentrated at lower incomes. A tax built on their transactions takes a larger share of income from families who can least afford it, which makes it regressive. It is also unequal for people in the same situation. Two workers cashing the same $800 paycheck would pay different amounts depending only on whether one of them has a bank account. And because the base is narrow and shrinking as more people move to bank accounts and payment apps, the revenue would be small and unpredictable. Ohio has spent years lowering these costs Ohio lawmakers and voters have worked for more than a decade to protect the same borrowers this tax would target: 1996: H.B. 313 let check-cashing businesses make small loans, with annual rates that could reach 390 percent or more (Schiff, 2022). 2008: H.B. 545, the Short-Term Loan Act, limited these loans to $500 with a 28 percent annual rate, and voters upheld it at referendum. Lenders then moved to other lending laws and credit services brokers, where fees were unregulated, and no lender licensed under the new law for the next ten years (Schiff, 2022). 2014: The Ohio Supreme Court ruled unanimously that payday-style loans made under the Mortgage Loan Act were allowed, which kept those workarounds open (Toledo Blade, 2014). 2018: The Ohio Fairness in Lending Act, H.B. 123, required payday-type lenders to license under the Short-Term Loan Law and capped total interest and fees at 60 percent of the amount borrowed. Supporters estimated Ohio borrowers would save more than $75 million a year (Bourke, 2018). A new tax on these customers would add back part of the cost the state has worked to remove. It could also push borrowers toward unlicensed online lenders, which hurts families and shrinks the revenue at the same time. Ohio can find school revenue in broad-based sources with low rates that do not single out families already paying the most for basic financial services. Part 2: Know your rights and your options If you or someone in your family is using a payday or short-term lender in Ohio, these protections and resources can help. The rules for licensed short-term loans in Ohio Under H.B. 123, loans from licensed short-term lenders must follow these limits (Ohio Legislative Service Commission, n.d.; Legal Aid of Western Ohio, 2020): Loan size: No more than $1,000, and no more than $2,500 owed to one lender at a time. Interest: No more than 28 percent per year. Monthly fee: No more than 10 percent of the loan or $30, whichever is less. Total cost: All fees and charges together cannot exceed 6

Every career pathway — healthcare, advanced manufacturing, the skilled trades, technology — begins with the ability to read, write, and communicate with confidence. For English language learners, immigrant and refugee families, first-generation students, and students with disabilities, that foundation is too often left to chance. W.I.S.E.C.E.O.’s literacy and language work brings research-based reading and language instruction to the learners and families who need it most, and equips the educators who serve them. It is the heart of our Education Access & Equity program — and the foundation under every workforce pathway we build. Family Literacy English Learners SIOP IEP & 504 Navigation Educator Learning 📖 Read together Fifteen minutes a day, in any language, builds the thinking skills that transfer to English. 🗣️ Talk to learn Structured conversation turns new words into real academic language. 🧩 Plan for every learner Language objectives, visuals, and sentence frames make lessons accessible to all. 🏛️ Know your rights Families who understand IEPs and 504 plans get the support their children deserve. What We Do How we build literacy. 👨‍👩‍👧 Family Literacy Practical guides and gatherings that help parents and caregivers build reading habits at home — in English or their home language — and connect reading to school and career goals. Families 🌐 English Learner Support SIOP-informed strategies, vocabulary and academic-language development, and resources for multilingual learners and newcomer students at every age. English Learners 🤝 Family Advocacy & IEP Navigation Plain-language workshops and guides that help families understand special education, IEPs, and 504 plans — including families who speak a language other than English. Families 🧑‍🏫 Educator Learning Practical strategies for teachers and paraprofessionals — differentiation, SIOP, and literacy across the content areas — so every classroom works for every learner. Educators 💼 Career & Digital Literacy Reading for the workforce: technical vocabulary, job applications, workplace communication, and the digital skills today’s employers expect. Youth & Adults 📰 Free Resources Family guides, teacher strategies, and policy updates delivered free through our newsletter. Registered apprenticeships let you earn a paycheck while you train for in-demand trades like electrical, welding, and advanced manufacturing. Apprenticeship.gov lists openings you can search by trade and location. Who qualifies: Career pivoters and job seekers who want hands-on work, plus local employers who want to train their own talent. Most programs accept ages 18+ (some 16+) with a diploma or GED. The path: Search Apprenticeship.gov for your trade and area, contact the program or employer, and apply. Once accepted, you work and train at the same time. Most programs last 1 to 5 years, and many skilled trades take about 4. The outcome: A paid position from day one, plus a nationally recognized credential when you finish. Your pay rises as your skills grow. Starting wages vary by trade and employer. Your action step today: Go to Apprenticeship.gov , select “Find Apprenticeships,” and search your zip code for one electrical, welding, or manufacturing program. C&I Tiffany Davidson is an educator, literacy advocate, and language-acquisition specialist who founded W.I.S.E.C.E.O. to open the doors that education opened for her. She holds two master’s degrees — in Literacy and Language Acquisition from the University of Cincinnati, and in Curriculum & Instruction from the University of Southern Mississippi — and a B.S. in English from the University of Southern Mississippi, along with certifications in TESOL and English Language Arts, and training in gifted and Section 504 services and administrative leadership. Her classroom work spans high schools in Ohio, Florida, and Mississippi. As ESL department chair and STEAM Club advisor at Western Hills High School in Cincinnati, she taught 150 multilingual students and mentored student STEM projects in partnership with TechOlympics and Amazon engineers. Before returning to the classroom, she spent more than a decade in business development, marketing, and financial services, experience she now brings to financial literacy education. Her work centers on the learners schools too often overlook: English language learners, immigrant and refugee families, first-generation students, and students with IEPs. As a literacy advocate, she helps teachers make every lesson accessible through research-based approaches such as SIOP and differentiated instruction, and she helps families understand and use their rights so their children get the support they deserve. At W.I.S.E.C.E.O., that experience powers our belief that literacy is the first job skill — and the foundation of economic mobility. text: Organizational Overview & Mission From the W.I.S.E.C.E.O. Knowledge Hub W.I.S.E.C.E.O. (Worldwide Institute For Success And Excellence) is an independent, community-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit that dismantles systemic barriers to technology, education and economic opportunity for underserved communities. It was founded and is led by educators with more than 30 years in the public school system. What is the mission? Our mission is to dismantle systemic barriers to technology, education and economic opportunity by giving underserved learners the skills, credentials and wrap-around support they need to build careers and lasting economic mobility. What is the vision? We envision a world where every learner, whatever their language, origin or zip code, has a real path to meaningful work, financial stability and leadership in their community. Who does W.I.S.E.C.E.O. serve? We serve learners historically underrepresented in technology and the workforce. That includes: Refugees and immigrants, including newcomer families and English learners Underserved students, high school age and older Underserved women and girls Veterans First-generation and low-income youth and adults seeking economic mobility Where does W.I.S.E.C.E.O. work? We are headquartered in West Chester, Ohio, with chapters in Kentucky, Florida and Mississippi. Our impact also reaches Georgia, Michigan, New York, Indiana, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Seattle, Washington, with learners from 35 nations. How are programs delivered? Programs are run by dedicated program staff, supported by trained volunteers and chapter leads, and delivered through our chapters and partner organizations. That network lets us enroll and support cohorts of 250 or more learners at a time. W.I.S.E.C.E.O. is not a school, a government agency or a religious organization. text: Digital Literacy Programs & Frameworks From the W.I.S.E.C.E.O. Knowledge Hub W.I.S.E.C.E.O.'s digital literacy work teaches coding, reading and digital skills to communities historically left behind. It rests on one belief: literacy is the first job skill, and the foundation of economic mobility. What is Digital Literacy & Coding? Digital Literacy & Coding brings coding, creativity and technology education to communities historically left behind, through app design, creative problem-solving and hands-on learning. Learners can join the waitlist . What is Literacy & Language Access? Literacy & Language Access brings research-based reading and language instruction to learners and families who need it most, and equips the educators who serve them. It is the heart of the Education Access & Equity program. It has five strands: Family literacy: guides and gatherings that help caregivers build reading habits at home, in English or their home language. English learner support: SIOP-informed strategies and academic-language development for multilingual and newcomer students. Family advocacy and IEP navigation: plain-language workshops on special education, IEPs and 504 plans, including for families who speak a language other than English. Educator learning: differentiation, SIOP and literacy across the content areas for teachers and paraprofessionals. Career and digital literacy: technical vocabulary, job applications, workplace communication and the digital skills employers expect. What approaches does the work use? The work uses research-based approaches, chiefly SIOP (the Sheltered Instruction Observation Protocol) and differentiated instruction. In practice that means language objectives, visuals and sentence frames that make lessons accessible to every learner. Who leads it? The literacy work is led by founder Tiffany Davidson, M.Ed. LSLS, M.Ed. C&I, who holds master's degrees in Literacy & Language Acquisition and in Curriculum & Instruction, plus TESOL certification. Knowledge Hub W.I.S.E.C.E.O.'s workforce programs connect learners to in-demand, high-wage careers through sector-based training, a no-cost career fellowship for high school students, and youth leadership development. What is the WISECEO Academy Career Fellowship? The WISECEO Academy Career Fellowship is the flagship program: a no-cost, industry-backed fellowship for grades 9–12 that trains students for jobs in cybersecurity, energy and infrastructure, and AI. Students can apply on the Programs page . What is Workforce Development? Workforce Development is sector-based training that aligns participants with in-demand, high-wage careers and connects them to competitive employers. Learners can join the waitlist . What is the Youth Leadership Academy? The Youth Leadership Academy cultivates diverse young innovators through technology immersion, leadership development and career pathways. Students can apply for a cohort . Which partners do learners work with? Students we teach and mentor take part in programs led by national, regional and civic organizations: Amazon Future Engineer: Amazon's childhood-to-career computer science and STEM program. AWS Community Engagement: technology education, volunteers and career exposure for local learners. TechOlympics: the nation's largest student-run technology conference, in Greater Cincinnati. DC Department of Employment Services: career pathways, technical training and apprenticeships. DC Council and civic leadership: youth development policy advocacy through the Jack and Jill of America On the Hill Legislative Summit. What career services are included? Every workforce learner can get resume help, interview preparation, job readiness training and connections to employers.
